@graph.headline: The History of Muhurat Trading: From 1957 to Today

acceptedAnswer.text: The first official Muhurat trading session was held on the Bombay Stock Exchange in 1957. The tradition itself is older: trading communities had long exchanged symbolic first trades and opened new ledgers at Diwali before any exchange formalised the practice. No primary circular from 1957 survives; the 1957 date is established by broad secondary-source consensus.

The Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) — Asia's oldest exchange, founded in 1875. BSE formalised the Diwali-session tradition in 1957, turning the trading communities' informal custom into an official exchange event.

mainEntity.name: Which exchange started Muhurat Trading first?

acceptedAnswer.text: The common shorthand is "since 1992" — but the precise answer is that NSE adopted the tradition as it came into operation. The exchange was incorporated in November 1992 and commenced trading in 1994 (wholesale debt in June, equities in November). It has carried the Muhurat session since its operational era began, taking it from the trading floor to nationwide electronic trading.

acceptedAnswer.text: Chopda Pujan is the Diwali ritual in which Gujarati, Marwari, and North Indian trading families worship new account books (chopdas): closing the old year's accounts, opening fresh ledgers with blessings of Lakshmi, Ganesh, and Saraswati, and writing auspicious first entries such as Shubh Labh. It is the religious-commercial root of Muhurat trading — the stock-exchange session is, in essence, the market's version of the ritual opening of a new year's books.

mainEntity.name: What is Chopda Pujan, and how is it related to Muhurat Trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because for India's trading communities, Diwali marks the fiscal new year. Merchant accounts were traditionally anchored to Kartik Pratipada, the day after Diwali, under the Vikram Samvat calendar (established in 57 BCE), and Gujarati New Year (Bestu Varas) falls the day after Diwali. A trading session at Diwali is the market's way of writing the first entry in the new year's ledger.

mainEntity.name: Why is Muhurat Trading held on Diwali?

acceptedAnswer.text: Muhurat means an auspicious time, chosen by astrology. The session's hour is set each year according to the Hindu panchang — the same astrological reasoning used to pick wedding dates, housewarmings, and new business launches. That is why the session's timings differ from year to year.

Honestly: there is no reliable data series behind claims that Muhurat sessions "often close positive" — such claims appear only in broker marketing, with hedged language and no cited statistics. The session's returns are ordinary market returns. The session is a ceremony at the opening of the trading year, not a source of expected outperformance, and no one should trade it expecting prosperity by ritual.

mainEntity.name: Has Muhurat Trading historically given good returns?

acceptedAnswer.text: Today, yes — equity, F&O (derivatives), currency, and MCX commodities all open for the Muhurat session. But the session did not start that way: it began as an equity-session ritual, and the derivatives segments (launched on NSE in 2000 for F&O and 2008 for currency) joined over the decades. The exact year each segment first participated is not documented; the multi-segment session is confirmed for the present day.
